It does not spin as one piece: the equator turns faster than the poles, and the rotation time quoted is for 16 degrees of latitude.
Sunspots and flares rise and fall in a cycle of about 11 years, and its magnetic field drives that.
unknown: Why the corona, the Sun’s outer atmosphere, is hundreds of times hotter than the surface beneath it is still being worked out.

Its axis is almost upright, so the floors of some deep polar craters never see sunlight.
unknown: How it ended up with such a large metal core for its size. Ideas include a giant impact that stripped away rock, but none is settled.

unknown: Whether any volcano is erupting now. Signs of recent lava flows have been reported, but activity is not confirmed.
How and when it lost its water, and whether it ever had a cooler, wetter past.

It turns once in about 23.93 hours, and its axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees, which is why there are seasons.

It has one natural satellite, the Moon, and no rings.
unknown: How and where life first began is still an open question.
The core and deep interior are probed only indirectly, by earthquake waves and magnetic measurements, so details of their makeup and heat flow remain uncertain.
Exactly how Earth gained its water (already present as it formed, or delivered later by asteroids and comets) is debated.

know: It was found by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930, and counted as the ninth planet until 2006, when the IAU created the class of dwarf planets.
It orbits in 248 years, on a path tilted 17 degrees and stretched enough that it sometimes comes inside Neptune’s orbit.
Its air is about 99% nitrogen with some methane, at roughly 13 microbar, 1/80,000 of Earth’s pressure.
It and its large moon Charon circle a point between them, and both show the same face to the other.
unknown: Whether a liquid ocean lies beneath the ice, as the shape and cracks of the surface hint.
How its atmosphere changes over its 248-year orbit, as it moves away from the Sun and refreezes.
How its five moons formed; a giant collision is the leading idea.

know: Spinning a large ring or cylinder so that its floor presses outwards, and feels like gravity, is a real idea studied since the 1950s.

Gerard O’Neill’s 1970s cylinder designs would be miles long and turn about once every two minutes.
unknown: No station of this kind has been built. The International Space Station is far smaller and does not spin.
The sphere, the engines, the shipyard and its engineers are inventions of the story.
